Enchanter
en-CHANT-er
noun
From the Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” from in- and cantare, to sing. The enchanter binds by uttered spell, close kin to the charmer; the modern “enchanting” scene has lost the dark labour the word once carried.

Biblical Definition

An enchanter works his art by incantation — the word is the Latin incantare, “to chant upon” a person or thing, from cantare, to sing. He is close kin to the charmer: both bind by uttered formula, and Scripture ranks them together among the arts by which the heathen sought to command the unseen. The law names him in the roll of the forbidden: there shall not be found among you “an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deu 18:10) — every one of them an abomination that drove the nations out of Canaan. When Jeremiah warns Judah not to trust the counsel that promised deliverance from Babylon, the enchanter stands among the false voices: “hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers” (Jer 27:9). Babylon herself was the seat of the art, and Daniel was schooled where the king kept “all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm” (Dan 1:20) — yet the captive who feared the LORD was found ten times wiser than the whole guild. And when judgment fell on that proud city, all her spells were powerless: her ruin came “for the great abundance of thine enchantments” (Isa 47:9). The enchanter multiplies words to master the world; the servant of God speaks one word of prayer to the Master of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who practices enchantment by magic incantation — from incantare, to chant upon.

ENCHANTER, one who enchants; a sorcerer or magician who uses spells and incantations.

From Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” from in- and cantare, to sing.

He is kin to the charmer, both binding by uttered formula rather than open force.

The law forbids the enchanter among the abominations of the nations (Deu 18:10).

Babylon fell for the great abundance of her enchantments (Isa 47:9).

Key Scripture

Deu 18:10 — "There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch,"

Jer 27:9 — "Therefore hearken not ye to your prophets, nor to your diviners, nor to your dreamers, nor to your enchanters, nor to your sorcerers, which speak unto you, saying, Ye shall not serve the king of Babylon:"

Isa 47:9 — "But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood: they shall come upon thee in their perfection for the multitude of thy sorceries, and for the great abundance of thine enchantments."

Dan 1:20 — "And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm."

Modern Corruption

The word has drifted to mean mere delight (“an enchanting evening”), while the thing itself has revived in the spell-craft and incantation of the modern occult.

expand to see more

The honest drift has hollowed the word: we call a lovely scene “enchanting” and forget that an enchanter was a man who chanted spells to bind souls and command spirits. But the live corruption runs the other way, restoring the old sense in earnest. The neo-pagan and “witchtok” revival teaches incantations, invocations, and chanted rituals as literal technique — the belief that spoken formulae can bend reality, heal, curse, or summon. That is incantare, the enchanter’s craft, and Scripture forbids it root and branch, not because the words are silly but because they reach for a power God has forbidden and open the soul to darkness.

The law lists the enchanter with the diviner and the witch and pronounces them all an abomination that emptied Canaan of its nations (Deu 18:12). Against every incantation stands the one word that Christians are given: “to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Babylon, the very academy of enchantment, was undone in a day for the abundance of her spells (Isa 47:9); and the captive Daniel, who used none of them but prayed to the God of heaven, outlasted the whole city. The lesson is fixed: the enchanter’s many words are wind, and the believer’s few words of prayer reach the throne.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word is incantare, “to chant upon” — a caster of magic spells, kin to the charmer.

expand to see more

Enchanter — from Latin incantare, “to chant upon,” via cantare, to sing.

He binds by spoken incantation, close kin to the charmer’s carmen.

The law forbids the enchanter among the abominations of Canaan (Deu 18:10).

Jeremiah ranks enchanters among the lying counselors of Judah (Jer 27:9).

Babylon, mistress of the art, fell for the abundance of her enchantments (Isa 47:9).

Usage

"In the AV an enchanter is a spell-caster, not a charming host; the law numbers him with the witch."

"The word is incantare, to chant upon — the enchanter binds by incantation, as the charmer binds by song."

"Babylon kept a whole guild of enchanters, and Daniel, who prayed instead, proved ten times wiser."
